newsitem.title: USA: Ill. House committee advances incinerator subsidy.
newsitem.headline: Ill. House committee advances incinerator subsidy.

text.p: An Illinois House committee has advanced a bill to provide at least $213 million in subsidies to a suburban Chicago waste-to-energy incinerator over 25 years.

The partly bond-financed incinerator developed by CGE Ford Heights in that south suburb was moth-balled last year while in the testing phase after lawmakers repealed a state subsidy that guaranteed a higher rate for electricity sold to public utilities.

Under the proposal, the incinerator would receive $1 for each tire burned and 3.3 cents for each kilowatt hour of electricity generated for an estimated $213 million, said Alexander Ewing, staff attorney for the Environmental Law & Policy Center, which opposes any incinerator subsidies.
The House Energy and Environment Committee voted 12-8 Wednesday to advance the plan sponsored by Rep. Michael Giglio, D-Lansing, in an amendment to an existing bill, a committee aide said.

The proposed amendment to a Senate bill must now pass a House vote by the end of business on Friday, a committee aide said. If it misses the deadline, the plan could still be revived in conference committees next week before the legislature adjourns.

CGE Ford Heights, which declared bankruptcy last year, had developed the facility through $79.6 million of bonds sold through the Illinois Development Finance Authority in 1994. A federal bankruptcy court agreement between the developer and bondholders allows for interest payments only on the bonds until Oct. 1.
The Giglio proposal follows other legislative attempts to restore incinerator subsidies that failed earlier in the session.
Developers of four incinerators have also filed court challenges to the retroactive repeal of the subsidies law. Only the Ford Heights facility and another in Robbins passed the design stage.
The Robbins incinerator developed by Foster Wheeler Corp was forced into a temporary shutdown last week when a construction permit allowing operation during an initial 180-day startup period expired.

The Illinois Pollution Control Board has permitted the incinerator to accept garbage from 12 municipalities with which it has contracted. It can sort the garbage for recycling purposes, but cannot burn it.
Illinois Environmental Protection Agency has set a June 2 deadline to determine whether the incinerator will receive an operating permit, spokesman Dennis McMurray said.
